passage: At the school sports club, the coach split everyone into relay teams. Sarika, new this term, stood at the edge fiddling with her hearing aid. Nobody called her name. Mridul noticed she watched people's lips when they talked. He walked over and faced her directly. "Want to be on our team? You can run third." She nodded, surprised. Before the race, he tapped her shoulder instead of shouting when it was her turn to get ready. She ran fast. After, she said quietly, "Thanks for looking at me when you talk." Mridul grinned. "You're quick. Stay with us next week too."

qa.q: What did Sarika fiddle with at the edge?
qa.a: She was fiddling with her hearing aid.

qa.q: What might Sarika's quiet thanks suggest about how she had been feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she had felt left out and was relieved someone made it easier for her to join.

qa.q: Which of Mridul's choices helped Sarika join in?
qa.a: He invited her, faced her when speaking and tapped her shoulder instead of shouting.

qa.q: How might the team see Sarika after the race?
qa.a: They may see her as a fast teammate, not just the new girl.

grounding: It shows a child making room for a new, shy classmate with a hearing aid.

passage: I'm Sahil, and Vidya sits in front of me. When the new boy came to our class on crutches, most of us just stared. At lunch he sat alone near the steps, because our usual spot is on the grass slope. Vidya picked up her tiffin, walked over and sat next to him. The next day she asked our group to move to the steps. A few of us grumbled. She didn't argue; she just went. I don't know if she felt sorry for him or just liked him. By the end of the week, all of us were eating on the steps, and he was telling jokes.

qa.q: Where did the new boy sit alone at lunch?
qa.a: He sat alone near the steps.

qa.q: What does Sahil think might have been on Vidya's mind?
qa.a: Sahil isn't sure if she felt sorry for the boy or simply liked him.

qa.q: What small step made the biggest difference for the new boy?
qa.a: Vidya moving to eat beside him, and then asking the group to move to the steps.

qa.q: How is the new boy affected by the end of the week?
qa.a: He is no longer alone and feels comfortable enough to tell jokes.

grounding: A classmate observes a child making room for a new classmate with different abilities.

passage:
Day one: Lakshmi joined Class 6 from Kerala. She hardly spoke and ate lunch alone, staring at her book. Dilnaz saw her but didn't know what to say.
Day four: At recess, Dilnaz walked over with a skipping rope. "We need one more to hold the rope. Want to?" Lakshmi hesitated, then took the end.
Week three: Lakshmi taught the group a clapping game from her old school. Everyone got the rhythm wrong and laughed. Lakshmi laughed loudest. Dilnaz noticed she'd started saying "we" instead of "you all."

qa.q: What did Dilnaz bring when walking over on day four?
qa.a: Dilnaz brought a skipping rope.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi saying "we" instead of "you all" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she now feels included and at home in the group, no longer an outsider.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz have done on day one?
qa.a: Dilnaz could have simply said hello or asked Lakshmi to join them at lunch.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi's clapping game change the group?
qa.a: The group enjoys something new she brings, which makes her a contributor, not just a newcomer. 😊

grounding: It shows a child including a shy new classmate over several weeks.

passage: Come, kanna, sit. When I was ten, a new girl joined our school in Madurai. Her name was Sarika, and she walked with two wooden crutches. At break, all of us ran to play kho-kho and she sat alone on the step, turning her bangles. Nobody was mean. We just forgot her. After three days I felt so bad I couldn't eat my lemon rice. So I went and asked, 'I'm Lavanya. Will you be our timekeeper? You have a watch.' She shouted the times louder than our teacher! Later we made up a sitting game with pebbles so she could win too. Sarika and I wrote letters to each other for forty years. That is what making room means, kanna.

qa.q: What job did young Lavanya offer Sarika at break?
qa.a: Lavanya asked Sarika to be the timekeeper for kho-kho because Sarika had a watch.

qa.q: Why couldn't young Lavanya eat the lemon rice?
qa.a: Lavanya felt guilty that everyone had forgotten Sarika, who sat alone on the step for three days.

qa.q: Which of young Lavanya's ideas worked, and why?
qa.a: They gave her a real role in the game and then invented a pebble game where she could play and win too.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt on those first three days at break?
qa.a: She probably felt lonely and left out, sitting by herself while everyone ran off to play.

grounding: An elder recalls making room for a new classmate who used crutches.

passage: Rain hammered the tin roof, so PE moved into the crowded school hall. Forty children shouted at once. Vikas noticed Deepak, the new boy with the hearing aids, standing by the wall looking lost. Sir had explained the relay rules, but in this noise Deepak had clearly caught nothing. Vikas walked over and stood right in front of him so Deepak could see his face. 'Relay. Run, touch the wall, come back, tap the next hand,' he said slowly, and showed it with his arms. Deepak nodded and grinned. 'Our team?' 'Our team,' said Vikas. When Deepak got tapped, he ran like wind. Afterwards he said, 'Thanks. Nobody faces me.'

qa.q: Where was PE held that day, and why?
qa.a: It was held in the crowded school hall because rain was hammering the roof.

qa.q: What does Deepak's comment 'Nobody faces me' suggest about how he felt before?
qa.a: It suggests he often felt lonely and left out, because people spoke without letting him see their faces, so he missed things.

qa.q: What small step made the difference for Deepak?
qa.a: Vikas stood face to face, spoke slowly and showed the rules with gestures before inviting him onto his team.

qa.q: What would have changed if Vikas hadn't walked over?
qa.a: Deepak would likely have stayed by the wall, confused about the rules and left out of the relay.

grounding: Shows a child including a new classmate with a hearing difference despite a noisy setting.
